description_full: Valero Energy Corporation manufactures, markets, and sells petroleum-based and low-carbon liquid transportation fuels and petrochemical products in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Latin America, Mexico, Peru, and internationally. It operates through three segments: Refining, Renewable Diesel, and Ethanol. The company produces California Reformulated Gasoline Blendstock for Oxygenate Blending (CARBOB) and Conventional Blendstock for Oxygenate Blending (CBOB) gasolines, CARB diesel, diesel, jet fuel, heating oil, and asphalt; feedstocks; aromatics; sulfur and residual fuel oil; intermediate oils; and sulfur, sweet, and sour crude oils. It sells its refined products through wholesale rack and bulk markets; and through outlets under the Valero, Beacon, Diamond Shamrock, Shamrock, Ultramar, and Texaco brands. The company also owns and operates renewable diesel and ethanol plants, as well as produces and sells renewable diesel, renewable naphtha, and neat sustainable aviation fuel under the Diamond Green Diesel brand name. In addition, it offers ethanol and various co-products, including dry distillers grains, syrup, and inedible distillers corn oil to animal feed customers. The company was formerly known as Valero Refining and Marketing Company and changed its name to Valero Energy Corporation in August 1997. Valero Energy Corporation was founded in 1980 and is headquartered in San Antonio, Texas.

financial_summary: Valero Energy Corporation is a large-cap energy business with a $105.9B market cap on $122.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -11% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 5.7×.

Shareholder yield of 3.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 165% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 39% and a beta of 0.72, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.52 vs 5y 0.58), so read it loosely.

val: The price sits above its blended-model fair value of $115 (margin of safety -231%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 9%).
On multiples it looks cheap against Energy peers: P/E 8.6 vs 13.6 and EV/EBITDA 5.2 vs 7.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 538% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an EBIT/EV of 2.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 19 covering analysts target $423 on average, 11% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 8.0%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.80).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.48x.

hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.8x net debt to EBITDA ($4.7B of cash against $10.6B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 5.7x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -11.4% over 3 years, 13.6% over 5 years and 3.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 36%).
At current returns, reinvesting 27% of profits supports about 2.7% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 11.5% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (1.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and institutions hold 88%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $7.7M sold).
It returns 3.8% a year to shareholders (2.5% in buybacks and 1.3% in dividends).

It has paid a dividend for 37 consecutive years, though it has been cut 2.6% a year over the last five.
